metadata.title: The Universe You Can Afford.
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro af_bella) - per-beat mp3 durations are MEASURED, never estimated

metadata.target_runtime: Under 3:00 BY DESIGN. The human asked for under three minutes on Ep. 06 after a 5:23 first cut, so this episode was WRITTEN to a word budget derived from Ep. 06's measured speech rate (0.3843 s/word) rather than trimmed afterwards. Predicted 2:51.
metadata.purpose: Ep. 07 of the AI in Astronomy & Space Science series, from weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md Astronomy topic 07 (Simulating the universe - AI-accelerated cosmological simulations replacing expensive N-body calculations).
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity palette. Terracotta #D97757 is the ONE accent and marks THE CHEAP ANSWER throughout - the Zel'dovich curve, the Zel'dovich panel, the approximation's error. Ink marks the expensive truth. That mapping is fixed for the whole reel so the viewer never re-learns which is which. Cosmic-web plates are bright-on-dark warm monochrome; the one line plot is ink-on-white.
metadata.distinct_from_earlier_episodes: Eps. 01-06 all had AI looking at OBSERVATIONS - triaging, classifying, detecting, deciding. Ep. 07 is the first where there is nothing to look at: you cannot run an experiment on the universe, so a theory's only voice is a simulation, and the AI's job is to STAND IN FOR THE PHYSICS rather than inspect data. The limit is correspondingly new - the emulator is trained on N-body output, so it is a compression of simulations already paid for and cannot be trusted outside that box. That is a circularity, not an accuracy ceiling (Ep. 04), an unseen class (Ep. 03), an irreversible rejection (Ep. 05) or a latency (Ep. 06).
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00, B11, B12, B13. Every other beat illustrates its concept as a reel-local Manim scene (scenes.py). All plates are generated by assets/gen_cosmos.py, which ACTUALLY RUNS both calculations the episode describes - a Zel'dovich displacement and a particle-mesh N-body solve in 2D - so the comparison on screen is a measured result, not an illustration. Every beat showing a plate captions it as a 2D toy at 512^2. No LaTeX/MathTex anywhere. metadata.channel_title is omitted for the GATE V edge-bleed reason logged in Ep. 03. scenes.py is ASPECT-AWARE: one file lays out 16:9 and the 9:16 derivative in short/.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about how AI is replacing the most expensive calculation in cosmology — simulating a universe — and what you give up when a network answers instead of gravity.

show.event: cream page; IRREDUCIBLY HUMAN eyebrow, then the serif segment title
spark + greeting Namaste, HAI settles above the composer card
the ask types itself into the composer; send button arms when it lands
terracotta running indicator: allocating 44,100 simulations...
three result lines stagger in - method, accuracy, limit. The ask lands ANSWERED.

props.command: Cosmologists test theories by simulating whole universes, and a proper test needs thousands of them. What is the actual method for replacing those simulations with a neural network, how accurate is it, and what does the shortcut cost?
output: method - skip gravity: correct a cheap linear guess with a network trained on real N-body runs
accuracy - within ~5% on the standard statistics, in a thousandth of the time
limit - it is trained on N-body output, so it cannot be trusted outside that box

beats.narration_text: This is Humanitarians AI. Six episodes about AI looking at data. This one, it replaces the physics.

show.event: top-left kicker: AI IN ASTRONOMY & SPACE SCIENCE - EP. 07
OM MALI draws on large, terracotta hairline sweeping under it
role line: Humanitarians AI - presenter
a panel sets two rows: 'six episodes: AI looks at the data', struck, then 'this one: AI replaces the physics' in the accented token
@HumanitariansAI wordmark bug settles bottom-right, inside title-safe

beats.narration_text: One breath. You can't experiment on the universe, so cosmology tests a theory by simulating it — and that takes thousands of universes. Nobody can afford it, so a network learns the answer instead.

show.event: a cosmic-web plate sits left, captioned as a 2D toy
kinetic type set one: NO EXPERIMENT IS POSSIBLE
set two: SO YOU SIMULATE IT
set three: THOUSANDS OF THEM, the count in the accented token
closer: so a network learns the answer instead

beats.narration_text: Why thousands? You aren't checking one universe, you're searching a parameter space. Quijote is forty-four thousand simulations across seven thousand cosmologies: eight and a half trillion particles, built as training data.

show.event: a 2D slice of parameter space draws on, two unlabelled axes
sample points scatter across it, one dot per cosmology
three counters land: 44,100 SIMULATIONS, 7,000 COSMOLOGIES, 8.5 TRILLION PARTICLES
a chip beneath, in the accent: BUILT AS TRAINING DATA

beats.narration_text: Each one is expensive because gravity has no shortcut. Every particle pulls every other, so you deposit mass on a grid, solve for the field, nudge everything, and repeat, hundreds of times.

show.event: the initial-conditions plate lands, captioned 2D TOY, 512 SQUARED
a loop diagram draws beside it: DEPOSIT, SOLVE, KICK, DRIFT
the loop closes and a HUNDREDS OF STEPS chip lands
closer: gravity has no shortcut

beats.narration_text: Here's the trick. There's a cheap answer — the Zel'dovich approximation. Move every particle once, in a straight line, and stop. Very good while the universe is smooth; badly wrong once things collapse.

show.event: one particle at rest, an arrow, one straight-line move: ONE MOVE, THEN STOP
the Zel'dovich plate arrives, framed in terracotta
two chips: RIGHT WHILE SMOOTH / WRONG ONCE IT COLLAPSES
closer: exact, right up until it matters

beats.narration_text: So you don't fix the physics, you fix the picture. Train a network on the difference between the cheap guess and the real simulation, then apply that correction. It never computes a force.

show.event: the terracotta Zel'dovich plate left, the ink N-body plate right
a minus sign lands between them and the residual plate resolves beneath
a network glyph takes the residual as its target: LEARN THE DIFFERENCE
closer: it never computes a force

beats.narration_text: It works. On the statistics cosmologists use — power spectrum, bispectrum, wavelets — the emulator matches N-body within about five percent at most scales. In a thousandth of the time.

show.event: the measured power-spectrum plate lands; the scene draws its axis labels
the two curves are named: N-BODY in ink, ZEL'DOVICH in terracotta
a bracket marks where they part company: THE NON-LINEAR PART
two figures land: WITHIN ~5%, and 1/1000 OF THE TIME

beats.narration_text: Now the design tell. That model has never simulated gravity. It learned the map from a starting field to a finished one, for the universes it was shown. Compression, not physics.

show.event: a card draws on: WHAT THE MODEL LEARNED
row one types in and is struck: THE LAW OF GRAVITY
row two lands in the accent: THE MAP FROM START TO FINISH
a bound box closes around it, labelled THE UNIVERSES IT WAS SHOWN
closer: compression, not physics

beats.narration_text: Which tells you where it breaks. The reported errors sit inside dense haloes — and haloes are where galaxies live. In my own two-D run, the cheap guess is four percent off on large scales and sixty on small ones.

show.event: the halo zoom pair lands: N-BODY left in ink, ZEL'DOVICH right in terracotta
a ring marks the core the cheap guess fails to build
a label: AND HALOES ARE WHERE GALAXIES LIVE
two measured numbers from this reel's own run: 4% LARGE SCALES, 58% SMALL

beats.narration_text: The deeper limit is quieter. Training it needs N-body runs, so it's a compression of simulations you already paid for, and you can only trust it inside the box it was shown.

show.event: a box draws on, labelled THE COSMOLOGIES IT WAS TRAINED ON
N-body runs pour in as ink dots; the emulator glyph sits inside
an arrow tries to leave the box and is struck through in terracotta
closer: a compression of what you already paid for

beats.narration_text: Recap. Cosmology can't experiment, so it simulates, and that needs thousands of runs nobody can afford. The emulator skips gravity and corrects a cheap guess: five percent, a thousand times faster.

show.event: the artifact page scales up on the cream stage, spark + title bar
four numbered recap lines stagger in, one per spoken clause

props.artifactTitle: The Universe You Can Afford - one page
props.artifactHeading: The method, and what it costs
artifactLines: There is no experiment. A theory's only voice is a simulation, and a real test needs thousands of them.
N-body has no shortcut: deposit mass, solve the field, kick, drift - hundreds of steps, trillions of particles.
The emulator skips gravity. It corrects the cheap Zel'dovich guess with a network trained on real runs.
Within ~5% on the standard statistics at a thousandth of the cost - inside the box of cosmologies it was shown.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this. I want to replace an expensive simulation with a learned surrogate. Help me choose which statistics it must reproduce and to what tolerance, how to spot an input outside its training set, and what I'd still run the slow way. Grade it: named tolerances, an out-of-distribution check, a slow-path audit.

show.event: spark + greeting 'Your turn.' - the one greeting that drops the persona
the suggested prompt types itself while the voice reads it verbatim
terracotta running line: paste this into Claude...
the three-item rubric staggers in as output lines

props.command: I want to replace an expensive simulation with a learned surrogate. Help me (1) choose which statistics it must reproduce and to what tolerance, (2) detect when an input falls outside its training set, and (3) decide what I would still run the slow way to keep it honest.
output: grade it: are the TOLERANCES named, per statistic
grade it: is there an OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION check
grade it: is there a SLOW-PATH audit that still runs
